title: The Evolutionary Origin of Predication and Syntax
content: The hypothesis assumes that predication originally corrected the addressee’s belief. But recent Theory-of-Mind studies suggest that understanding another’s false belief develops late in ontogeny, unless grasped through the linguistic communication of the person holding that false belief. Could this understanding arise in evolution from non-predicative communication? Evidence that dolphins and elephants use sounds “to call a particular companion over” may support this possibility. Hominins probably had similar signals. But for hominins, unlike dolphins and elephants, understanding another’s false belief may have been almost within reach. Thus, hearing another group member call someone known to be well beyond calling range, one hominin recognizes the caller’s false belief. But developing predication was difficult. The call had to become a referential sign to which a correction, supplement, or update was added. Moreover, a two-word intonation pattern (an embodied resource for facilitating the unification of the syntactic composition) had to develop gradually, requiring articulatory-phonetic sequences constant across the sign’s different uses. Recent research on animals’ inability to learn sequences would support this requirement’s late emergence.
